summary.en: The infinitive, the three present-tense patterns, biti and imati, negation and asking questions.
summary.bs: Infinitiv, tri obrasca prezenta, biti i imati, negacija i postavljanje pitanja.

en.one: The infinitive (infinitiv) is the dictionary form of the verb. It ends in -ti or -ći.
en.explain: -ti: raditi (to work), čitati (to read), pisati (to write), piti (to drink). -ći: ići (to go), moći (can), doći (to come), peći (to bake). It's used after other verbs: 'Volim čitati', 'Moram ići'. In Croatian the infinitive is strongly preferred; in Bosnian you'll often hear 'da + present' instead: 'Moram da idem' (Moram ići).
en.why: You need the infinitive for modal verbs, for the future (radit ću) and to look up any verb.
en.mixup: The infinitive doesn't show the stem clearly: pisati → pišem, ići → idem. Learn the 'ja' form together with the infinitive.

en.one: The present tense (prezent) has three main patterns, named after the 'ja' ending: -am, -im and -em.
en.explain: -am (čitati): čitam, čitaš, čita, čitamo, čitate, čitaju. -im (raditi): radim, radiš, radi, radimo, radite, rade. -em (pisati): pišem, pišeš, piše, pišemo, pišete, pišu. The endings for ti (-š), mi (-mo) and vi (-te) are always the same; only the vowel changes. The present covers both 'I work' and 'I'm working'.
en.why: One tense does the job of two English ones, and the endings tell you who's acting, so you can drop the pronoun.
en.mixup: Don't build -em verbs from the infinitive: pisati → pišem (not pisam), ići → idem, piti → pijem.

en.one: 'Biti' (to be) has short forms you use constantly and long forms for emphasis and questions.
en.explain: Short (unstressed): sam, si, je, smo, ste, su. Long (stressed): jesam, jesi, jest(e), jesmo, jeste, jesu. Negative: nisam, nisi, nije, nismo, niste, nisu. Short forms can't start a sentence: 'Umoran sam' or 'Ja sam umoran', never 'Sam umoran'. 'biti' also helps build the past: radio sam (I worked).
en.example: 'Ja sam iz Bihaća. Jesi li ti student?' – 'Jesam.' / 'Nisam.'
en.why: Short forms of biti are the most common words in the language and they follow the special 'second position' rule.
en.mixup: Answering a question with just 'Sam' is wrong. Use the long form: 'Jesam' (Yes, I am).

en.one: 'Imati' (to have) follows the -am pattern, and its negative is one word: nemati.
en.explain: imam, imaš, ima, imamo, imate, imaju. Negative: nemam, nemaš, nema, nemamo, nemate, nemaju. 'Ima' and 'nema' also mean 'there is / there isn't': 'Ima li kafe (kave)?' After 'nema' the thing goes in the genitive: 'Nema hljeba (kruha).'
en.example: 'Imam dvoje djece.' 'Nemam vremena.' 'U sobi nema nikoga.'
en.why: 'Nema' with the genitive is one of the most frequent patterns, and your first real use of the genitive case.
en.mixup: Don't say 'ne imam'. The negative is fused: 'nemam'.

en.one: To negate a verb, put 'ne' right before it, written separately: ne radim, ne znam.
en.explain: Three verbs fuse with ne: biti → nisam, imati → nemam, htjeti → neću. Double negatives are normal and required: 'Ne znam ništa' (I don't know anything, literally I don't know nothing). 'Niko (nitko)', 'ništa', 'nikad', 'nigdje' always come with 'ne' on the verb.
en.example: 'Ne pijem kafu (kavu).' 'Nisam umoran.' 'Nikad ne idem tamo.' 'Neću!'
en.why: Negation is essential, and the double negative is the opposite of the English rule, so it needs practice.
en.mixup: 'ne' is written separately from verbs ('ne znam'), but together with nouns and adjectives when it forms a new word: neznanje, nesretan.

en.one: Yes/no questions are made in three ways: with 'da li', with verb + 'li', or just by intonation.
en.explain: 1. Da li + statement: 'Da li radiš danas?' (common in Bosnian, less in Croatian). 2. Verb + li: 'Radiš li danas?' (standard in both). With biti: 'Je li on tu?', 'Jesi li gladan?' 3. Intonation only: 'Radiš danas?' Question words: ko (tko), šta (što), gdje, kada, zašto, kako, koliko, koji, čiji.
en.example: Bosnian: 'Da li imaš vremena?' Croatian: 'Imaš li vremena?' Both: 'Gdje živiš?'
en.why: You'll ask questions constantly, and recognising both styles helps you understand speakers from both countries.
en.mixup: Croatian standard avoids 'da li je' and uses 'je li': 'Je li to istina?' Bosnian accepts both.

explain.en: pisati is an -em verb with a stem change: pišem.

q.en: How do you say 'I don't have time'?

explain.en: imati fuses with ne (nemam), and the thing goes in the genitive: vremena.

q.en: Which answer to 'Jesi li umoran?' is correct?

explain.en: Short forms can't stand alone. Use the long form: Jesam.
Double negation is required: nikad + ne.
